O'BRIEN vs DAWLEY The First Great Rivalry in Visual Effects BY STEPHEN CZERKAS

O'Brien vs Dawley The First Great Rivalry in Visual Effects BY STEPHEN CZERKAS INTRODUCTION BY DON SHAY In the firmament of visual effects superstars, few have burned brighter than Willis O Brien, whose seminal work in stop-motion and other cinemagical techniques influenced and inspired generations of visual effects professionals. By extension, it also influenced and inspired the creation of Cinefex. A fan of King Kong since my first childhood viewing on television, I began researching the life and work of Willis O'Brien in 1962, shortly after he passed away. I was in college at the time, long before the Internet and Google revolutionized research, but I managed to make contact with O'Brien's widow, Darlyne, who provided a wealth of personal and professional information on her late husband, and put me in touch with the people she knew who had worked with him. Much of what I accumulated over the next decade of intermittent research appeared in an article I wrote for the now-defunct British journal, Focus on Film. A decade after that, I expanded it into a full-issue biography of O'Brien that appeared 1 / 22 in Cinefex 7. For 30-plus years, that article has remained the definitive record of

O'BRIEN VS DAWLEY O'Brien's life and career, and the root source (sometimes credited, often not) for just about everything that has been written about him since. No one else, it seemed, had the resources or determination to uncover much more about him. Until recently. Willis O Brien was clearly the hero of my story, but every good hero needs a villain, and that role was assigned to producer Herbert M. Dawley. As etched into the historical record by my long-ago article, Dawley approached O Brien in 1918 with the idea of collaborating on a picture. O'Brien had recently completed a series of prehistoric stop-motion shorts for The Edison Company, and Dawley was interested in producing a more ambitious dinosaur film. O Brien jumped at the opportunity. Their joint venture, The Ghost of Slumber Mountain, was a success, and O'Brien went on to join producer Watterson R. Rothacker on a feature-length adaptation of Arthur Conan Doyle's The Lost World, which was to cement O'Brien's reputation as the undisputed master of stop-motion animation. But there were complications. Dawley, with apparent malice, removed O'Brien's technical credit from the theatrical release of Slumber Mountain, then proceeded to make another dinosaur movie without him, Along the Moonbeam Trail, a long-lost film thought to have been cobbled together using outtake animation from their earlier venture. Even more damning, or so it seemed, Dawley had sought and obtained a patent for the innovative stop-motion armatures used in those films, and when news was made public that The Lost World was going into production, sought an injunction to derail the film on the basis of patent infringement, claiming that his former employee, O'Brien, had essentially 2 / 22 stolen his work.

O'BRIEN VS DAWLEY My account of this episode was based on the personal recollections of Darlyne O'Brien - who had not yet met her husband at the time these events transpired - and on newspaper articles and various affidavits and court documents I was able to acquire in the course of my research. That account remained unchallenged for 30 years. Enter Stephen Czerkas. Stephen is an artist and a sculptor who worked in stopmotion for many years, perhaps most notably on Planet of Dinosaurs. Since then, he has created life-size dinosaurs for museums, authored books and scientific papers on dinosaurs and their relationship with birds, and, with his wife, Sylvia, founded The Dinosaur Museum in Blanding, Utah. A number of years ago, he turned his inquiring mind to the question of what really happened between Willis O Brien and Herbert Dawley, and in the course of his research, came up with some startling findings that cast a new light on their bitter dispute - one that suggests Dawley has been sadly maligned all these years. In part to set the record straight, or at least amend it, I invited Stephen to share some of his discoveries with Cinefex readers and recount the fascinating story of how he came upon them. His full account will appear in a book-length biography of Herbert M. Dawley, slated for publication later this year. 3 / 22

O'BRIEN VS DAWLEY t began some years ago with a photograph. I found it on an Internet auction, and to prevail over my bidding rivals, I paid far more than I could rationally justify, but I knew it was important to the history of stop-motion animation. The photo was of Herbert M. Dawley taking a model of a dinosaur out of a plaster mold. I was aware, at once, that there was something strange about this early silent-era image. What the photo showed was that the model was not built in the fashion that Willis O'Brien had been known to employ, by shaping modeling clay over a metal armature, then skinning it with sheets of rubber dental dam and adding surface details. Instead, it must first have been sculpted out of clay, over which a plaster mold was made to produce a casting from some sort of pliable material. What I found intriguing was that since O'Brien would not have used this process to create the animation model, it suggested that Dawley might have been much more influential in the making of The Ghost of Slumber Mountain - whose dinosaurs were generally attributed solely to O'Brien - and to his long-lost follow-up film, Along the Moonbeam Trail, done without O'Brien, which animation historians had long speculated was compiled from outtakes of the earlier film. Since the creature in the Dawley photograph was a duck-billed dinosaur - one not used in The Ghost of Slumber Mountain - it seemed most likely that the photo was attributable to Along the Moonbeam Trail. The possibility remained that the model could have been made for the first film and used in the second, but the prospect that Dawley actually made and animated the models for the second film was a teasing alternative. With Along the Moonbeam Trail being a lost film about which little was known, there 4 / 22 was no way to prove that Dawley was responsible for the animation and O'Brien was not,

but I was curious to learn more. O'BRIEN VS DAWLEY On the Internet, I found an obscure reference to Dawley's having co-founded, in 1922, a community theater in Chatham, New Jersey, where he lived. To my surprise, that theater - which Dawley had served as director until his death in 1970 - was still in operation. I contacted the theater's current president, Chris Furlong, explained my interest in Dawley, and, acknowledging that it was a long shot, asked if there might be any documentation or photographs relating to Dawley's movie career stored somewhere at the theater, maybe up in the rafters. I had heard of old posters being found in similar situations in movie theaters, so I thought it was worth a try. Chris thought it highly unlikely, but he agreed to have a look. A day or two later, he called me back, very excited. "It was just like you described. I found it all. Scrapbooks filled with photos and clippings, hand-written diaries, and ... are you sitting down? There's a box of metal film cans. I unspooled the ends just far enough to see what I could, and on one reel, there was a dinosaur!" Remarkably, the film appeared to have no noticeable signs of wear or deterioration, but since it dated back to the 1920s, we realized that the film stock was nitrate-based and could be very flammable and dangerous to handle. We decided to donate the films to the Academy of Motion Pictures Arts and Sciences, with the understanding that they would properly transport them to their facility in Hollywood, take measures to insure that they were preserved, and provide a digital copy for the theater and one for myself to be used in a documentary I envisioned on Herbert Dawley. 5 / 22 Once the films were digitally transferred, I had the opportunity to watch them for

the first time. Surprisingly, there was unedited footage of actors wearing costumes dating back to biblical times. There were also complete and incomplete examples of animated silhouette films Dawley had made with Tony Sarg, the renowned illustrator and master of marionette puppetry. Shot in black-and-white, they had been tinted in color to enhance the effect of day or night. But the most important reel was that with the dinosaur footage, which turned out to be, not from The Ghost of Slumber Mountain, but rather Along the Moonbeam Trail, long believed to have been lost forever. Only the second half of the two-reeler was in the found footage, but that included all of the film's dinosaur sequences. The animation was competent, smooth and lifelike, for the most part. Included was footage of a flying pterodactyl, a stegosaur, a tyrannosaur - and the duck-billed dinosaur from the fateful photograph that had led me on this quest. It was still difficult to be certain at this point, but the notion that O'Brien had been responsible for the dinosaurs in Dawley's second film appeared increasingly unlikely. tographs and scanning. The Dawley scrapbooks contained photos of his family, his childhood, his adult life, both personal and professional. There were even entire sections devoted to The Ghost of Slumber Mountain and Along the Moonbeam Trail, with clippings, photographs and theatrical pressbooks. For several days, I documented everything I could via pho6 / 22

The Dawley diaries - six loose-leaf binders filled to capacity with neat, hand-written entries in blue ink - covered the last 12 years of his life in remarkable detail. As such, they did not relate directly to his early moviemaking days. While randomly flipping through one of them, however, I happened upon a newspaper clipping stapled onto the page. It was an obituary on Willis O'Brien. I was stunned. After so many years, the relationship between the two men had been recorded in this gesture of finality. Immediately below the clipping, and continuing on the following page, Dawley wrote a brief remembrance of the man who had worked for him long ago. First, he observed that O'Brien had been a "clever but undependable" worker, but then added a detail that was, perhaps, even more revealing about the nature of their estrangement. For some reason, not elaborated, O Brien was away when it came time for his then wife, Hazel, to give birth to their first child. And with the soon-to-be father unavailable, it was Herbert Dawley who not only drove Hazel to the hospital but also ended up paying her medical expenses. At the time of the journal entry, Dawley mused that the child would now have been 44 years old, which revealed his unawareness of the tragic episode in O'Brien's life in which both of his young sons were slain by their mother. As I went through his scrapbooks and read the diaries, I came to realize that Herbert M. Dawley was a most remarkable man. Prior to becoming a filmmaker, he spent ten 7 / 22 years with Pierce-Arrow - a luxury automobile manufacturer of the era - as an artistic

designer and engineer, and is still held in high regard among automobile historians. He even held patents on some of his automotive innovations. The Ghost of Slumber Mountain was his first film, but he went on to make others, serving not only as a hands-on producer, but also an actor and director. He was a painter and a sculptor, a civic-minded individual respected for his dignity and integrity, and a distinguished Army officer attached to the New Jersey Militia. In short, Dawley did not fit the profile of a person likely to seek credit for someone else's work. So what happened between him and Willis O'Brien? Except for their interest in stop-motion animation, the two men had little in common. Even their personalities were very different. Dawley was gregarious, secure and outgoing, whereas O'Brien, while fun-loving, tended to be withdrawn and insular, often avoiding social interactions. Evidence would suggest that O'Brien was not satisfied working for Dawley, whose small start-up company was no match for the once-omnipotent Edison studio, now in financial straits, where O'Brien had done his earlier stop-motion films, and that O'Brien was looking to advance his career elsewhere, even as work proceeded on The Ghost of Slumber Mountain. Rothacker and Cathrine Curtis. Watterson R. Rothacker was a prominent film industrialist whose company provided laboratory developing and print duplication services for motion pictures. He was also active in making films, more for the purposes of advertising than entertainment. However, after meeting with O'Brien, who explained that he could re-create living dinosaurs on film, Rothacker saw the potential of this unique form of animation, and the two men decided to embark on an adaptation of Arthur Conan Doyle's The Lost World. With O'Brien under contract, Rothacker acquired rights to the property, but then, unwilling or unable to assume the day-to-day responsibility of producing a feature motion picture, sought and secured a financial and production partnership with Cathrine Curtis, an actress and independent producer. First, I focused on Cathrine Curtis, whose personal and professional papers I found archived at the University of Wyoming, Laramie. I spent days feverishly documenting everything of note, particularly her communications with Rothacker, but also O'Brien and Dawley. What I found began to fill in many gaps in the puzzle. Then, a year or so later, I located Barry O'Neil, the grandson of Watterson Rothacker, who, as luck would have it, had two wooden crates filled with oversize scrapbooks containing clippings and photos covering his grandfather's entire life and career in motion pictures. Another treasure trove. What had begun as a modest endeavor had snowballed 9 / 22 exponentially. After assimilating the archives of Herbert Dawley, Cathrine Curtis and Wat-

terson Rothacker, I now had answers to at least some of the gnawing questions inspired by that perplexing photo of Dawley and his duck-billed dinosaur. employee's claim that it was he who was responsible for the film and its technical achievements, to Paul H. Cromelin, president of The Inter-Ocean Film Company. It was May 1919, and Cromelin had just closed a deal with Herbert Dawley to distribute The Ghost of Slumber Mountain, which had been previewed at the Strand Theatre in New York the previous November. Rothacker was intent upon blocking the film's wide release. When that maneuver failed, Rothacker followed up with a barrage of ads in industry trade publications that included a five-paragraph statement in which O'Brien asserted that he alone was responsible for the work in The Ghost of Slumber Mountain, that a printed program from the Strand Theatre preview supported his claim that he was the producer of the film, and that he was now an employee of the Rothacker Film Manufacturing Company, which controlled all rights and interest in his process and current productions. The ads further proclaimed that O'Brien had already completed i a number of these extraordinary productions - they're great; decidedly better than anything Mr. O'Brien ever did before. It is doubtful, if not naïve, to think that O'Brien was so distraught about not getting screen credit on Slumber Mountain that Rothacker would go to such trouble and exO'BRIEN VS DAWLEY he charge that Dawley failed to give O'Brien screen credit on The Ghost of Slumber Mountain - true, if not without provocation - came from O'Brien himself in a sworn affidavit that Rothacker sent, together with a letter asserting his new 10 / 22

What was much more important was that they were claiming the process of stop-motion animation to be exclusively under their control - a key condition in the advancement of their still-secret plans to bring The Lost World to the screen. Contrary to the ad copy, O'Brien had completed no productions, extraordinary or otherwise, under the Rothacker banner. That claim was strictly a smoke screen. Dawley responded to the initial salvo with a three-page letter to Cromelin in which he provided a detailed account of how the production had come about and what transpired during the making of it. Satisfied with Dawley's accounting of the facts, the distributor went ahead with the theatrical release of The Ghost of Slumber Mountain, which proved to be a financial success. Had Dawley not written the letter defending himself - and retained a copy for his files - his film might well have been scuttled, and only his adversaries' side of the story would have survived for historical scrutiny some 90 years after the fact. Dawley began his letter by expressing surprise "that a man of Mr. Rothacker's business sagacity would permit an employee of his to make a sworn statement without first having more thoroughly investigated the facts." He then went on to acknowledge that while the program for the Strand Theatre's showing of the film listed O'Brien as producer, he was, in fact, nothing of the sort. "(The program) does give O'Brien credit for being the producer," Dawley wrote, "but if you will run the original positive now in your possession you will see that he is given credit for the photography and mechanical effects. This I1 / 22 announcement on the program is erroneous and was printed before I had seen it or I

should have taken steps to have the statement corrected. However I was disposed at that time to feel that O'Brien would act in good faith as an employee of mine who had been accorded considerable more courtesy in the way of publicity than he was entitled to. Subsequent events proved that this assumption on my part was wrong. Within the letter, Dawley described how he, prior to knowing O'Brien, had constructed a model of a brontosaur over a jointed skeleton and then photographed it using a pocket Kodak still camera to create a series of photos, which he then assembled into a flip-book on whose pages the dinosaur appeared to browse among the foliage of a miniature set and to walk across the screen." Dawley showed the primitive test to his cousin, J. Searle Dawley, a prolific director for The Edison Company. Impressed by what he saw, J. Searle encouraged Herbert to carry on with his idea about doing a film involving dinosaurs. Thus inspired, Herbert Dawley spent a month studying dinosaurs with two paleontologists at the American Museum of Natural History, examining skeletons and analyzing how the legs would have moved, in order to animate the dinosaurs for his film. Dawley asserted that he supervised O'Brien closely while he worked on the models and that, for the sake of expediency, some joints were provided by O Brien, who already had them from his previous work. Everything was subject to Dawley's direction, he insisted, and often he had to instruct O'Brien to make corrections. At the time, Dawley was still active in the New Jersey Militia, and on occasion had to report for duty. At one point, he asserted that he left O'Brien on his own to animate while he was away. O'Brien completed about 100 feet of film, but when Dawley returned, he thought the footage was unacceptable, and threw it out. iI then went into the studio and took active charge of the work, doing the animation while he turned the crank of the camera. From then on he did not do anything without my actual presence at the time, or without my having first planned the action and by frequent inspection directed its progress. Even the proper lighting of the set was the result of my arrangement." Dawley's letter continued with his explanation of the credit dispute. The original version of the film consisted of about three reels, but Walter Hayes, manager of the Strand Theatre, considered it too long, and stipulated that it needed to be shortened to a single reel prior to its premiere engagement. Dawley determined what footage needed to be removed, and then left the actual cutting and reassembly to O'Brien, which, to those at the theater, gave the impression that O'Brien was very much responsible for doing most of the work on the film. 13 / 22 Why did Dawley delegate the final edit of his film to O'Brien, an employee whose

O'BRIEN VS DAWLEY talent and work he disparaged? On October 4, 1918 - between the September completion of the longer version of the film and the November debut of the shorter version at the Strand Theatre - a catastrophic explosion occurred at the T.A. Gillespie Ammunitions Plant, in Morgan, New Jersey, where massive amounts of munitions were manufactured and stored during World War I. Approximately 100 people were killed in the blast, hundreds more were injured, and thousands were evacuated from nearby communities. The devastation was enormous. "Blast at Gillespie Plant Wrecks the Whole Town" proclaimed a banner headline in a local newspaper. As commander of the 4th Battalion of the New Jersey Militia, Major Herbert M. Dawley was called into action to orchestrate the disaster response. Exhausted from the overwhelming task of supervising the recovery, during which he averaged only about one hour of sleep for eight days straight, Dawley was physically unable to re-edit his film and get everything ready for the premiere. Consequently, he had little choice but to entrust O'Brien with the final edit and with other mundane chores such as seeing that the theater program was printed correctly. After O'Brien completed his work, Dawley gave him a hundred-dollar bonus, and offered free use of the equipment and leftover film for any commercial work that he might procure. In trying to be fair and maintain a good working relationship, Dawley went so far as to offer O'Brien a percentage of the profits should the film be successful. Also, according to Dawley in his letter to Cromelin, he had given O Brien a greater credit than he deserved. So he was totally blindsided when he learned that the theater program O'Brien had printed up listed O'Brien as the film's producer. 14 / 22 Only after that incident did Dawley discover that O'Brien had met with Watterson

O'BRIEN VS DAWLEY Rothacker during production on The Ghost of Slumber Mountain, and was planning to leave Dawley to work for Rothacker in Chicago. After showing Rothacker examples of the work he had done for Edison, Rothacker had asked if O'Brien could provide a more refined example of his work. In his letter to Cromelin, Dawley implied that O Brien, without his knowledge or permission, had shown footage from Slumber Mountain to secure his new position. Angered by O'Brien's blatant disloyalty, and by his attempt to take more credit than he deserved, Dawley severed all ties with his former employee and deleted his screen credit from the film. T hile o Brien continued to develop the still-secret Lost World project with his new benefactor, Dawley set about producing Along the Moonbeam Trail entirely on his own. As in his first picture, he took the main acting role himself, and employed the same two children, Chauncey and Alan Day, now noticeably older. This time, he had two assistants, including his father, John Dawley, and a talented artist, Charles C. Horn, who worked mostly on construction of the miniature sets and as a helping hand. Dawley himself made the dinosaur puppets and did all of the animation. Having engineered jointed puppet armatures that he considered much more advanced and sophisticated than those used in Slumber Mountain, Dawley shrewdly applied for, and was granted, a patent for the design of his articulated creations, essentially staking his claim to the stop-motion process. Along the Moonbeam Trail was a two-reeler, which ran about half an hour. Although 15 / 22 the first reel of that long-lost fantasy adventure was missing from the treasure trove dis-
